newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: No "special region" status for East Timor, minister.
newsitem.headline: No "special region" status for East Timor, minister.

text.p: Indonesian Foreign Affairs Minister Ali Alatas on Tuesday said that Jakarta did not see granting East Timor "special region" status as a solution to the troubled territory and former Portuguese colony.

"I don't think that that (special region status) is one solution that the Indonesian government is contemplating at this time," Alatas told reporters during a visit to Abu Dhabi, capital of the United Arab Emirates.

The United States, the United Nations and the Vatican have this week called for a speedy settlement to the future of East Timor which was invaded by Indonesia in 1975 and annexed the following year in a move not recognised by the U.N.

Jamsheed Marker, the recently-appointed U.N. special envoy for East Timor, visited the territory last weekend for the first time, and said he believed there was "a desire and, God willing, a possibility (for a solution)".
"Special region" status has historical precedent elsewhere in Indonesia.
A possibility of Jakarta giving up its sovereignty on East Timor was "not on the cards," Alatas said in Abu Dhabi.
"I don't think we can at this stage already speculate in what direction the solution is," he added.
U.N.-sponsored talks between former ruler Portugal, which is demanding self-determination for the East Timorese, and Indonesia have been deadlocked for nearly 15 years.

"We think that Portugal should be realistic enough to see that what happened 20 years ago cannot be turned back. They cannot turn back the clock," said Alatas, adding that Lisbon had simply abandoned the former colony.
Official Indonesian sources have said the integration of East Timor into Indonesia is an accomplished fact and Indonesian President Suharto has rejected "autonomy" for the territory.
Thirty-three East Timorese entered the Austrian embassy compund in Jakarta on Tuesday, demanding a meeting with Marker who had a three-day visit to East Timor.
"Why have they gone into the embassy? Because it draws the attention of journalists. They are entitled to go to the U.N. offices in Jakarta but not on their terms," Alatas said.
East Timor residents and human rights groups estimate that about 200,000-250,000 people have died in East Timor since the 1975 invasion, a subsequent invasion and two decades of strife.
